South Korea also says it deployed fighter jets, while Taiwan says it "responded" to Russian military aircraft detected in their respective air defence identification zones. These are unofficial buffer areas beyond territorial airspace where governments identify approaching aircraft for security purposes. Moscow has yet to comment. The alleged incursions are a reminder of Russia's military power ahead of the Apec economic summit in China this week, which Vladimir Putin will attend alongside US President Donald Trump. Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said the flight paths of the Russian aircraft, off the south-western Okinoshima island, were a "serious infringement of Japan's sovereignty" and "completely unacceptable". DeWitt characterized people of Japanese ancestry during World War II. He insisted that even those who had been born and raised as U.S. citizens nevertheless posed a threat because their Japanese “racial strains” were “undiluted.” Under the authority of President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s Executive Order 9066, DeWitt ordered the removal of all Japanese Americans from the West Coast in 1942. Allowed to take only what they could carry, they were imprisoned, without trial, in some of the most desolate places in the country. Today, the National Park Service preserves those sites so that visitors may learn their story. Jeffrey Novak Principal Deputy General Counsel Novak was appointed Principal Deputy General Counsel in May 2025 and served as Acting General Counsel until October 2025. He is an Honors College graduate of Ball State University and a graduate of the Indiana University School of Law. During law school, Novak worked as a law clerk for Bill Cummings, formerly the United States Attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia. After graduating law school, he served a two-year clerkship with the late Charles R. Richey, United States District Judge for the District of Columbia, before joining McGuire Woods, where he was elected to partnership. Before joining the Department, he worked in a variety of roles at technology companies over the course of more than 20 years, including managing litigation, compliance, patent, and public policy functions, while also serving on the boards of the Northern Virginia Technology Council, the Internet Association, and the Virginia Early Childhood Foundation.

pages.description: Gas bills will increase by about 5% from 1 December, Island Energy announces.
pages.text: Jersey gas bills to rise as Middle East turmoil persists Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Gas bills to rise as Middle East turmoil persists 6 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Jonathan Morris Channel Islands Press Association Island Energy said customers can contact its customer team for support Gas customers in Jersey will see their bills increase by about 5% from 1 December after Island Energy announced a rise in tariffs for households and businesses. The company said its mains gas, mini bulk tank and cylinder tariffs would increase by 1p per kilowatt hour (kWh) for all domestic and commercial customers from 1 December 2026. It said the increase reflected higher wholesale gas and liquefied petroleum gas costs amid disruption to exports and shipping routes in the Middle East after the conflict with Iran. Chief executive Graeme Millar said: "We recognise that any price increase is unwelcome, particularly during winter." More news stories for Jersey Listen to the latest news for Jersey Securing fuel at lower prices in advance had limited the impact of wholesale cost increases on customers, Millar said. However, the energy boss added: "It cannot fully protect customers from sustained increases in the cost of fuel and bringing it to Jersey." Island Energy said customers concerned about paying their gas bills could contact its customer team to discuss what support might be available. Follow BBC Jersey on X , Facebook and Instagram . Close jfd553's Diary Mapping Icefields Parkway, Part 1: A two-year mapping journey Posted by jfd553 on 4 November 2026 in English . Last updated on 6 November 2026. I spent two years mapping the areas surrounding one of the most beautiful drives in the world. Each morning, I looked forward to discovering and mapping an area adjacent to a one I did the day before. This diary entry serves as an introduction to a series of texts covering the challenges I encountered and how I overcame them. Included below are a few snapshots taken in the field, which capture the majestic landscapes along the Icefields Parkway. I have also added a “before and after” map excerpt, as well as a short video, to illustrate how my work gradually took shape over time. The Place The Icefields Parkway (Highway 93N), in Alberta, owes its name to the spectacular icefields and glaciers that line the road. The parkway, which is a 232 km stretch of highway cutting through Banff and Jasper National Parks, attracts between 1.2 million and 2 million visitors per year. The parkway offers exceptional alpine landscape, with glaciers, rivers, turquoise lakes, and breathtaking mountain views directly from the roadside (Figure 1). Best of all, many of these landmarks can be reached in a single day’s hike (Figure 2). Figure 1: North Saskatchewan River alongside the parkway. Veils of seaweed hung from its rotting timbers, and it was encrusted with barnacles. The insides were full of mud. Richard Mukuze By Sam Kemp Published November 18, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). The jazz saxophonist Stan Getz once said that the best music sounds “like a good conversation among friends”. Right now, some of the most interesting musical conversations in London are happening at its grassroots venues, where open jam sessions are giving musicians of all levels a platform to improvise, hone their craft and form new friendships. Participants may not know their fellow musicians, let alone the genre or dynamic, so there’s no choice but to embrace whatever the night brings. It’s about getting lost in music, together. London’s open jam scene really took hold in the years following the Covid lockdown — a period when music-lovers were looking for new ways to connect in a city beset by independent venue closures and the ongoing effects of social isolation. New Zealand's Southern Alps are home to one of the world's rarest birds: the black stilt. Natasha Bazika By Natasha Bazika Published June 11, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). Clouds move quickly across the Mackenzie Basin, dragging shadows over braided riverbeds and dry tussock plains that stretch towards New Zealand’s Southern Alps. One moment, the landscape is washed silver; the next, it disappears beneath a sweep of weather rolling over the mountains. I’m heading deeper into this high country on a window of borrowed time, crossing the 46,950-acre wilderness of Glenmore Station, a merino sheep, deer and cattle station. Hours earlier, the same storm front had grounded my helicopter flight to the country’s highest whisky bar — The Bad Decision, on a saddle above Glenmore Station — before it could leave the tarmac. Now, I’m racing a temporary clearing in the weather to find something far more elusive than a dram of mountain liquor: the black stilt, or kakī in Māori, one of the rarest birds on the planet. “The Mackenzie Basin has its own weather system,” says guide Ben Laffan, who’s taking me on Tekapo Adventures’ Black Stilt birding tour , a newly launched birdwatching experience, directing our four-wheel drive up a rough track. pages.text: Josh Kerr: The Making of the Man Behind the Shades - BBC Sport By Richard Winton BBC Sport Scotland You know Josh Kerr, right? The guy with the shades. The fastest man to ever run a mile. Scottish, but with a curious transatlantic accent. Slicked-back hair. Beard. Usually got a medal of some kind slung around his neck. No stranger to telling you what he thinks. That's Kerr the competitor, one of the foremost faces in world athletics, and a man who rampaged around London's Olympic Stadium in three minutes 42.66 seconds in July to set a new world record - then followed it up with a home Commonwealth gold and an imperious triumph at the Ultimate Championship. Kerr recognises the description, smiling as it's articulated. But is there another version of him? Speaking to him during one of his regular returns to Scotland from his New Mexico base, it becomes clear there is. There's scant chat about records, medals and his enjoyably niggly rivalry with Jakob Ingebrigtsen. Instead, he talks about disguising alcohol-free cider, entering races under a false name, cold-calling universities, being starstruck meeting Scotland's rugby players and his granny keeping him humble. This is the Kerr who spent the thick end of an hour on a chilly August evening taking selfies, signing his name and sharing his wisdom with young fans at Scotstoun after his Commonwealth medal presentation. pages.description: The animals that plummeted 85 feet into Wyoming’s Natural Trap Cave provide a layered history of life dating back to the Pleistocene
pages.text: Journey Into a Prehistoric Cave That Trapped and Entombed Animals for Millennia Skip to main content Illustration by Emily Lankiewicz / Photos courtesy of Dr. Susumu Tomiya and public domain Natural Trap Cave is a pit in northern Wyoming into which countless animals have fallen and met their untimely demise since the Pleistocene. Paleontologists today find the cave a treasure trove — a stunning record of the species that have long roamed the area. The mammalian fossils left behind shed light on the climate, food sources and migration patterns of these species from earlier eras. Careful excavation work over the years that has involved sifting for bones, extracting ancient DNA, and looking for prehistoric pollen has revealed not just the plants and animals that once populated this part of the world, but also the ecosystems and climates that governed it. It also has required some rather advanced rappelling skills. In this episode, host Ari Daniel speaks with vertebrate paleontologist Julie Meachen and Smithsonian contributing writer Michael Ray Taylor about what rappelling into Natural Trap Cave reveals about its contents and what it can tell us about Earth’s past. Juanes & Mon Laferte: Tiny Desk Concert May 23, 2018 5:00 AM ET Felix Contreras Credit: NPR Colombian pop star Juanes and Chilean singer Mon Laferte recently wrapped up a sold-out tour of the United States, which (lucky for us) included a stop at the Tiny Desk. Laferte began the concert solo with the torch song "Pa' Dónde Se Fue" (Where Did You Go?). She sang the break-up story with a smirk that belied the heartache hiding in her poignant lyrics. Then, after a short set break starring the Tiny Desk engineer Josh Rogosin, Juanes joined her to perform the duo's sultry single, "Amárrame" (Tie Me Up). It's rare to see Juanes in such an intimate setting. After almost two decades of performing solo, the Latin pop star is more of a stadium and arena kind of guy. It's a treat to hear his voice unencumbered by loud speakers or crowd noise, and to see his facial expressions as he sings lyrics that many of us know by heart. This marked a return to the intimacy that fueled his earliest days and that's still present in the personal lyrics that have sold millions of records. This weekend, I was at State of the Map 2026, the international OpenStreetMap conference, which took place in Paris this year. Here’s a brief, personal feedback and a round-up of a few presentations that stood out for me. You can also find all the videos at https://peertube.openstreetmap.fr . NB: there is a French version here . This one was translated with the help of DeepL translate. The most inspiring: cartes.app Inspiring: cartes.app is a slightly mad project aimed at creating a new Google Maps, but without its car-centric bias. It started with a single contributor, but he’s managed to build a strong team around him: he has the insight to use the best open-source software components for his project – MapLibre for map navigation, vector tiles for map rendering, Photon for geocoding, and Transitious for public transport. Today, the developer is no longer working alone: he is securing funding and attracting contributors from around the world to improve his app and translate it so it can reach a global audience. It’s a wonderful project worth supporting, and you can do so by subscribing to cartes.app premium for just €1 a month. Jungle: Tiny Desk Concert November 2, 2026 5:00 AM ET Robin Hilton Credit: Photo: Lexy Beale/NPR It's hard for any band to make the old sound completely new, but Jungle has spent much of the past decade transforming vintage soul and R&B into something almost alien. The grooves are deep and warmly familiar, with wistful reflections on love and longing. But even in the brightest moments, there's often a thread of mystery and melancholy that leaves you questioning whether everything is as it seems. Fronted by the trio of Tom McFarland, Josh Lloyd-Watson and Lydia Kitto, Jungle is known for fluid live sets, with songs that spill into each other. True to form, at the Tiny Desk, they perform more than a half-dozen tracks that run together in a single, continuous groove. pages.text: Jurassic period information and facts | National Geographic SCIENCE What is the Jurassic period and why did it end? The heyday of dinosaurs, the Jurassic era saw Earth’s climate change from hot and dry to humid and subtropical. The Jurassic period was characterized by a warm, wet climate that gave rise to lush vegetation and abundant life. Many new dinosaurs emerged—in great numbers. Above, Dimorphodon reptiles fly over a herd of Mamenchisaurus dinosaurs coming down to a river for a drink. Illustration by CoreyFord, Getty Images By National Geographic Staff Last updated August 18, 2025 The Jurassic is a geologic period that took place about 201.3 million years to 145 million years ago and constitutes the middle part of the Mesozoic era . The Jurassic period was named after the Jura limestone deposits in the Jura Mountains, discovered by German geologist Alexander von Humboldt . Building on this find, French scientist Alexandre Brongniart later coined the Jurassic period. There are three Jurassic time periods: early, middle, and late. Overall, the Jurassic gives us a particularly well-preserved fossil record of prehistoric life, which included theropod dinosaurs that scientists believe evolved to become birds . Thanks to this rich record, we know that the Jurassic was the age of dinosaurs roaming a tropical Earth filled with ferns, flowering plants, and conifers. It was also a time when sea monsters, sharks, and blood-red plankton filled inland seas borne of crumbling landmasses. Here’s what the Jurassic period was really like. pages.text: Justice Outcomes Explorer (JOE) Justice Outcomes Explorer (JOE) Skip Navigation Justice Outcomes Explorer (JOE) May 01, 2024 The Justice Outcomes Explorer (JOE) is a Census Bureau experimental data product that measures the economic and health outcomes of people who have been involved with the criminal justice system. Criminal justice involvement can include criminal charges, prison releases, and probation and parole sentences. Outcomes measured include employment, earnings, government program participation, and mortality. JOE is a collaboration between the U.S. Census Bureau and the University of Michigan that uses Criminal Justice Administrative Records System (CJARS) data to better understand how people involved in the justice system reintegrate into society. JOE covers criminal justice system involvement at any point between 2000 and 2020. Actual coverage of justice involvement depends on the coverage of agencies in the CJARS data, while coverage of outcomes depends on the availability of source data at the Census Bureau. Data users can download JOE data below or interact directly with the JOE data using the data visualization tool hosted by the University of Michigan. The tool includes additional justice-related outcomes created from CJARS without Census Bureau data. There are more miles of singletrack, more places to camp and dedicated space for races and other large events, all part of a broader effort by the Bureau of Land Management and community partners to keep pace with one of western Colorado’s busiest recreation areas. This fall, the final trail in the North Fruita Desert Trails Master Plan is complete. K2-Play winds for about three miles along the base of the Book Cliffs and completes the final phase of a roughly 30-mile expansion of the 18 Road trail system. Its completion caps years of planning and construction involving the BLM Grand Junction Field Office, Colorado Plateau Mountain Bike Trail Association, Mesa County, City of Fruita, local businesses, professional trail builders and volunteers. Keishaa Austin Keishaa Austin is the Associate Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary of the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE)’s Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation. Previously, she has served in other roles at DOE including as the Principal Deputy Director of the Office of State and Community Energy Programs (SCEP). Austin brings to DOE an extensive background in energy and communications. She served as a senior public utilities regulatory analyst in grid planning and reliability at the California Public Utilities Commission, and a program analyst at the Office of the People’s Counsel for the District of Columbia. She has also held roles with media and entertainment companies including Urban One, BET Networks and Capitol Music Group. Austin earned her law degree at Texas Southern University and her bachelor’s degree from Howard University.

pages.description: Usman Khawaja's autobiography has exposed the limbo Australian cricket finds itself stuck in over the sandpaper scandal, writes Stephan Shemilt.
pages.text: Khawaja book: Sandpapergate a stench Cricket Australia cannot shake - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Pat Cummins has led Australia in 43 Tests since 2021 By Stephan Shemilt Cricket Correspondent Published 10 November 2026 There are stories that can damage reputations, tarnish legacies and put asterisks next to achievements. Never-ending sagas, claim and counterclaim, one word against another. Are Pep Guardiola's trophies at Manchester City rendered worthless by financial rule breaches? Would either of the Houston Astros or Boston Red Sox have won the World Series without sign stealing? How much fake blood was spilled by Harlequins? Now, sandpapergate has morphed into Usman Khawaja's-book-gate, opening old wounds and asking questions that have hung over Australian cricket since Cameron Bancroft hid some DIY equipment in his jockstrap in 2018. Published on Tuesday, Khawaja's autobiography – Sabr – is only suggesting what plenty have suspected for the past eight years. It always seemed likely that Bancroft, Steve Smith and David Warner were not the only three members of the Australia camp with knowledge of the sandpaper plot. Careful with his words, perhaps for legal reasons, Khawaja has said enough to reignite a row that once consumed the entire nation of Australia. Crucially, the former batter has not named individuals and, in the opinion of Cricket Australia (CA), not presented enough evidence to merit a new investigation. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites. https://www.nist.gov/si-redefinition/kilogram/kilogram-kibble-balance SI Redefinition Kilogram: The Kibble Balance Named after its inventor, Bryan Kibble at the U.K.’s National Physical Laboratory (NPL) , who conceptualized it in 1975, the Kibble balance is an exquisitely accurate weighing machine. Like any balance, it is designed to equalize one force with another: In this case, the weight of a test mass is exactly offset by a force produced when an electrical current is run through a coil of wire immersed in a surrounding magnetic field. The surrounding field is provided by a large permanent magnet system or an electromagnet. The moveable coil, once electrified, becomes an electromagnet with a field strength proportional to the amount of current it conducts. When the coil's field interacts with the surrounding magnetic field, an upward force is exerted on the coil. The magnitude of that force is controlled by adjusting the current. Basic principles of the Kibble balance, a device that can be used to measure mass. Credit: Suplee/NIST The instrument was originally called a "watt” balance because it makes measurements of both current and voltage in the coil, the product of which is expressed in watts, the SI unit of power. Kimberly Ballou Kimberly Ballou serves as Chief of Staff for the U.S. Department of Energy’s Office of International Affairs (IA), a role she resumed in June 2026 after previously serving in the position during a period of leadership transition in early 2025. She has more than two decades of experience advancing U.S. international energy policy, global energy security, strategic partnerships, and international cooperation. Throughout her career, Kimberly has held senior leadership positions across IA, including Senior Advisor for Strategic Operations to the IA Assistant Secretary, Acting Director for Asian Affairs, Deputy Director for American Affairs, and Senior Advisor for Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean. Kimberly has also served in multiple overseas leadership assignments as Acting Energy Attaché and DOE Office Director, including at the U.S. Embassy in Paris, France; U.S. Embassy in Mexico City, Mexico; and U.S. Mission to the OECD in Paris, where she represented DOE and advanced engagement with foreign governments and key multilateral organizations, including the International Energy Agency and Nuclear Energy Agency. pages.description: The King Range National Conservation Area (NCA) is a spectacular meeting of land and sea as mountains thrust straight out of the surf with King Peak (4,088 feet) only three miles from the ocean.
